detail.longDescription: I am debugging a custom decoder-only Transformer that I train from scratch / continue pretraining in PyTorch. The current model has 159,674,112 trainable parameters with the following configuration: vocab_size = 32768 context_length = 1024 d_model = 768 n_layers = 18 n_heads = 12 n_kv_heads = 4 head_dim = 64 ffn_hidden = 2560 dropout = 0.0 RoPE theta = 10000 The architecture uses: decoder-only causal attention RMSNorm RoPE Grouped-Query Attention (12 query heads / 4 KV heads) SwiGLU PyTorch scaled_dot_product_attention tied token embedding / LM-head weights no linear biases After the latest continued-pretraining session, validation cross-entropy is finite and reasonably stable across several sources: FineWeb-Edu: 3.8058 DCLM-Edu: 3.6926 Wikipedia: 3.6084 Cosmopedia: 3.3566 FineMath: 3.3966 Training loss also behaves normally and I do not see NaNs, exploding loss, or obvious divergence. However, qualitative autoregressive generation from this model family has been much weaker than the loss would suggest: responses can become irrelevant, malformed, repetitive, or strongly fixated on a narrow pattern/domain. I am trying to determine whether this can be explained by model/data quality alone, or whether there may be a correctness issue that cross-entropy validation does not expose. The relevant part of my current attention implementation is: class CausalSelfAttention(nn.Module): def __init__(self, cfg: AbleConfig): super().__init__() assert cfg.n_heads % cfg.n_kv_heads == 0 self.n_heads = cfg.n_heads self.n_kv_heads = cfg.n_kv_heads self.head_dim = cfg.head_dim self.kv_repeat = cfg.n_heads // cfg.n_kv_heads self.dropout = cfg.dropout self.q_proj = nn.Linear( cfg.d_model, cfg.n_heads * self.head_dim, bias=False, ) self.k_proj = nn.Linear( cfg.d_model, cfg.n_kv_heads * self.head_dim, bias=False, ) self.v_proj = nn.Linear( cfg.d_model, cfg.n_kv_heads * self.head_dim, bias=False, ) self.o_proj = nn.Linear( cfg.n_heads * self.head_dim, cfg.d_model, bias=False, ) def forward(self, x, rope_cos, rope_sin): B, T, _ = x.shape q = ( self.q_proj(x) .view(B, T, self.n_heads, self.head_dim) .transpose(1, 2) ) k = ( self.k_proj(x) .view(B, T, self.n_kv_heads, self.head_dim) .transpose(1, 2) ) v = ( self.v_proj(x) .view(B, T, self.n_kv_heads, self.head_dim) .transpose(1, 2) ) q = apply_rope(q, rope_cos, rope_sin) k = apply_rope(k, rope_cos, rope_sin) if self.kv_repeat != 1: k = k.repeat_interleave(self.kv_repeat, dim=1) v = v.repeat_interleave(self.kv_repeat, dim=1) y = F.scaled_dot_product_attention( q, k, v, attn_mask=None, dropout_p=self.dropout if self.training else 0.0, is_causal=True, ) y = ( y.transpose(1, 2) .contiguous() .view(B, T, -1) ) return self.o_proj(y) The Transformer block is pre-norm: class TransformerBlock(nn.Module): def __init__(self, cfg: AbleConfig): super().__init__() self.attn_norm = RMSNorm(cfg.d_model, cfg.rms_eps) self.attn = CausalSelfAttention(cfg) self.ffn_norm = RMSNorm(cfg.d_model, cfg.rms_eps) self.mlp = SwiGLU(cfg) def forward(self, x, rope_cos, rope_sin): x = x + self.attn( self.attn_norm(x), rope_cos, rope_sin, ) x = x + self.mlp( self.ffn_norm(x) ) return x and the final model forward pass is essentially: def forward(self, idx): B, T = idx.shape if T > self.cfg.block_size: raise ValueError( f"sequence length {T} > " f"block_size={self.cfg.block_size}" ) x = self.tok_embeddings(idx) cos = self.rope_cos[:T] sin = self.rope_sin[:T] for block in self.blocks: x = block(x, cos, sin) return self.lm_head(self.norm(x)) For generation, I currently re-run the complete context rather than using a KV cache. The relevant sampling logic is: @torch.no_grad() def chat( self, messages, temperature=0.7, top_p=0.9, top_k=50, repetition_penalty=1.08, max_new_tokens=128, ): ids = self.tokenizer.encode( self._prompt(messages), add_special_tokens=False, ).ids[-(self.cfg.block_size - 1):] generated = [] for _ in range(max_new_tokens): context = (ids + generated)[-self.cfg.block_size:] x = torch.tensor( [context], dtype=torch.long, device=self.device, ) logits = self.model(x)[:, -1, :].float() if repetition_penalty != 1.0: for tok in set(generated[-128:]): value = logits[0, tok] logits[0, tok] = ( value * repetition_penalty if value < 0 else value / repetition_penalty ) if temperature <= 0: next_id = int( torch.argmax(logits, dim=-1).item() ) else: logits = logits / temperature if top_k > 0: k = min(top_k, logits.size(-1)) threshold = torch.topk( logits, k ).values[:, -1, None] logits = logits.masked_fill( logits < threshold, float("-inf"), ) probs = F.softmax(logits, dim=-1) if 0 < top_p < 1.0: sorted_probs, sorted_ids = torch.sort( probs, descending=True, ) cumulative = torch.cumsum( sorted_probs, dim=-1, ) remove = cumulative > top_p remove[:, 1:] = remove[:, :-1].clone() remove[:, 0] = False sorted_probs = sorted_probs.masked_fill( remove, 0.0, ) sorted_probs /= sorted_probs.sum( dim=-1, keepdim=True, ) pick = torch.multinomial( sorted_probs, 1, ) next_id = int( sorted_ids.gather(-1, pick).item() ) else: next_id = int( torch.multinomial(probs, 1).item() ) if next_id in {self.end_id, self.eos_id}: break generated.append(next_id) return self.tokenizer.decode( generated, skip_special_tokens=True, ).strip() One complication is that my latest checkpoint is a continued-pretraining/base checkpoint , while earlier qualitative generation tests were performed on an SFT/chat branch of the same architecture. Therefore I do not expect a base model to behave like a strong instruction-following assistant. What I am trying to distinguish is a weaker but correctly implemented model from an implementation bug. What sanity checks would be most useful for separating these cases? My current ideas are: Overfit a very small token sequence and verify near-perfect next-token prediction. Compare teacher-forced logits with logits obtained while growing the same sequence autoregressively. Run greedy decoding ( temperature=0 ) to remove sampling as a variable. Verify tokenizer encode -> decode and special-token round trips. Compare the loss of a sequence with the per-token log probabilities obtained from the same forward pass. Compare the custom GQA implementation against an equivalent MHA/reference implementation on a tiny deterministic model. Test RoPE independently with fixed tensors. Compare FP32 inference with FP16 inference. Is it possible for a decoder-only Transformer to obtain validation cross-entropy around 3.3-3.8 while still having an attention/RoPE/tokenization/inference bug that only becomes obvious during free-running autoregressive generation? More specifically, are there invariants for a causal LM where teacher-forced and autoregressive execution should produce numerically identical next-token logits, which I can use to prove that the inference path is correct before investigating data quality and undertraining?
